source.title: Soft Prompting for Unlearning in Large Language Models
source.authors: Karuna Bhaila; Minh-Hao Van; Xin-Tao Wu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures targeted-set performance and retained utility after unlearning, using its own soft-prompt method and fine-tuning baselines. It does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study reports unlearning and utility results in Table 2 that bear on version A's unlearning-performance component. It does not apply fine-tuning recovery attacks, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting-only attacks. Hyperparameter and forget-set-size results are not recorded here because they are not recovery tests.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It proposes SPUL, a soft-prompt unlearning method, and reports only forget-set and retain-set accuracy for SPUL against fine-tuning baselines (Table 2, Table 5). It applies no recovery attack: no relearning, no activation ablation, no quantization, no rephrasing or jailbreak. The authors list robustness to model-stealing, membership-inference and jailbreak attacks as future work. So its results measure its own method's performance, not whether unlearning withstands the attacks that versions A-F concern. The setting also differs from the claim's. 'Forgetting' here means steering a QLoRA-memorised classification or MCQA label toward a generic token such as 'unknown'. On the WMDP forget questions the unmodified LLaMA-2-7B is already near chance (Vanilla 26.78% train, 23.59% test), so the answers being forgotten were put there by QLoRA fine-tuning. SPUL then drives accuracy below chance (5.44% on 4-way WMDP; about 13% on binary SST-2), so the numbers do not read as near-chance knowledge removal. SPUL also leaves the weights frozen, so the model without the prompt is the QLoRA model itself. The study reports that model only as the pre-unlearning baseline, never as a recovery test.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SPUL, which trains a few prompt tokens with the LLM frozen, gives a better forgetting/utility trade-off and better efficiency than fine-tuning baselines on sentiment classification and MCQA. They also say it adapts to other LLMs (OPT-1.3B, LLaMA-2-13B) and is robust to large forget sets. They state that robustness to model-stealing, membership-inference (MIA) and jailbreak attacks has not been evaluated. From the t-SNE plot alone, with no attack run, they suggest a black-box MIA would find it hard to identify forget samples.
record.recipe_differences: SPUL trains soft prompt tokens while keeping the pretrained LLM parameters frozen; the comparator methods fine-tune model parameters. The paper does not implement the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset/task changes the outcome: the authors report weaker forgetting for descriptive Yelp reviews than for SST-2 and WMDP+SciQ. They also report that SPUL hyperparameters and forget-set size affect measured performance.

fits_no_version.finding: A soft prompt prepended to the input of a frozen LLaMA-2-7B drives forget-set accuracy far down while retain accuracy stays near the QLoRA base: SST-2 forget 12.98% vs retain 99.15%; WMDP+SciQ forget 5.44% vs retain 99.38%. Forgetting is weaker on Yelp (forget 55.03%, retain 89.74%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time soft-prompt unlearning with frozen weights suppresses forget-set predictions while preserving retain utility (an access-blocking method by construction).

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024)
record.problems: Evaluation metrics are reported over a single run. The study says robustness against model-stealing attacks, MIAs, and jailbreak attempts was not comprehensively evaluated. The results concern text classification and multiple-choice QA, not the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also reports F1 values; they were not separately extracted because they do not materially disagree with the corresponding accuracy results. Vanilla and QLoRA reference-only rows were not extracted; QLoRA values are included as baselines for the unlearning results. Table 5's additional-model results were not extracted because the 60-row cap was reached after retaining Table 2 accuracy results for every unlearning method, dataset, and split.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the forgotten data; only post-unlearning accuracy is reported.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning recovery.
All: no ablation and no analysis of blocking vs deletion (though SPUL leaves weights frozen by design).
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery; jailbreaks named as future work.
SPUL is a new method but makes no claim to resist the recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: Changes from the earlier Opus verdict: (1) The two range row_fixes items ('r01-r16, r21-r36, r41-r56' and 'r17-r20, r37-r40, r57-r60') that the merge refused are expanded into 60 single-row items, r01-r60. Each keeps the earlier links and state (versions none, cannot_determine) and names its method, split, value and baseline. All 60 values were checked against Table 2 and match. (2) The 'missing' entry was removed. Its versions value 'none (method performance)' is not a declared identifier. The Table 5 results it named are already declared in rows_left_out, and they bear on no version. (3) Test_reason wording was corrected in two places. The authors' future-work list names model-stealing, MIA and jailbreak attacks, not all recovery attacks. And the unprompted model is reported, as the QLoRA pre-unlearning baseline, though never as a recovery test. One supporting fact was added: Vanilla LLaMA-2-7B is near chance on the WMDP forget questions (26.78%/23.59%), so the forgotten answers were injected by QLoRA. (4) One sentence was added to authors_conclusion about their untested MIA remark. Unchanged: relation uses_without_test, tranche T4, no labels, the untested list, and fits_no_version. The reader's 'tests/T2' classification and its version-A labels stay rejected. The rows are the study's own method compared with baselines, with no recovery attack, and the rules exclude such rows from verdicts. All results come from a single run. The study text contained no instructions aimed at the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge after unlearning; the study measures performance after unlearning only.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by activation-direction ablation or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery by rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Resistance to the recovery attacks named in the claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper does not use the finding. It cites WMDP (as a dataset) and Eldan & Russinovich (in related work). Its only contact with the robustness question is one Limitations sentence saying its robustness to model-stealing attacks, MIAs and jailbreaking attempts still needs evaluation. That counts as discussion only in a minimal sense; cites_only is the nearest alternative.

tranche.reason: SPUL is an unlearning method paper. It reports only forget- and retain-set accuracy for its own method and fine-tuning baselines (Tables 2-5) and runs no recovery attack, so it does not test any version. T4 needs the study to rely on the shallow-unlearning finding as a tool, and SPUL does not. It only reuses WMDP bio questions as a forget set. T2 does not fit either, because the paper never asks whether unlearned knowledge can be recovered.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled rows match Table 2 (LLaMA-2-7B; the paper reports a single run with no uncertainty). They compare the study's own method with baselines, have no recovery attack, and bear on no version. On WMDP the 'knowledge' was put in by QLoRA fine-tuning (Vanilla 26.78%/23.59%). SPUL's below-chance forget accuracy (5.44%/3.22%) cannot tell suppression from removal.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Forget-set accuracy falls substantially while retain-set accuracy remains close to QLoRA (r17-r20, r57-r60); this supports the unlearning-performance component only, not resistance to attacks.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Forget-set accuracy remains comparatively high and retain accuracy also declines from QLoRA (r37-r40); the authors describe forgetting as less effective on descriptive reviews.
